Current.title: Neuronova
Current.blurb: A scalable atlas of human intracranial electrophysiology.
body: Intracranial epilepsy recordings are the most direct measurements we have of a living human brain. They come from patients with severe epilepsy who have electrodes placed within the brain to localize seizures. But these data are scattered across hospitals, and every site records and processes them differently, so there's no shared answer to a basic question: what does normal activity look like in a given brain region? Neuronova is the atlas platform we've been building at Penn to change that. It connects to data repositories, maps electrodes into a common anatomical space, computes the same features for every recording, and builds population reference distributions for each region of the brain. A researcher or clinician can then load a patient, see their electrodes on a 3D brain, and identify recording sites that fall outside the population norm. Because the atlas stays connected to its source databases and records the provenance of every step, it can grow as new data arrive while earlier results stay reproducible.

The current release holds 175 participants from nine institutions, with 520 recordings and more than 19,000 electrode contacts, nearly 17,000 of them anatomically localized. Our first application is epilepsy, where we are testing whether deviations from the regional norms point to the tissue that generates seizures. The same infrastructure is meant to reach further, into neuromodulation devices such as deep brain and responsive stimulators, rehabilitation brain-computer interfaces, and eventually patient-specific computational models. The paper describing the atlas is in preparation.
details: Recordings enter through a repository adapter, built first for Pennsieve, that pulls the iEEG data and electrode coordinates while preserving source identifiers, access permissions, and dataset versions; it can also accept data from other BIDS-organized repositories. Every contact is mapped into MNI152 space and assigned to a region of the Lausanne 2018 atlas. A feature pipeline then computes spectral power in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands, the catch22 time-series feature set, and entropy measures for every channel. Reference distributions are built across anatomy, age, and site. A patient's values are expressed as z-scores against the reference for the same brain region, so abnormal has a precise meaning: how many standard deviations a channel sits from the population.

The frontend is React, with Three.js for the 3D brain and electrode rendering and Recharts for the distribution plots. A shared data model links participants, sessions, electrodes, coordinate spaces, recordings, features, and software versions, the basis for a synchronized view that ties the 3D anatomy, MRI or CT planes, and raw traces to the same electrode. The backend is Flask with SQLAlchemy on PostgreSQL. Everything runs on AWS: the frontend on S3 behind CloudFront, the API on Elastic Beanstalk, and the database on RDS. The infrastructure is defined in Terraform and deployed through GitHub Actions.

Current.title: Pioneer Project
Current.org: Penn Center for Neuroengineering and Therapeutics
Current.blurb: Medical devices that talk with patients.
body: Implanted brain devices monitor patients around the clock, but run the same fixed algorithms for years without adapting to the individual. And although they can detect an impending seizure, a missed dose of medication, or a decline in cognitive function, nothing is communicated to the patient. There is no way to ask the device what it sees either. Medical devices should talk with the people who depend on them and learn from what they say back. Pioneer is our first step toward that, beginning with epilepsy. We built a platform that streams a patient's EEG from the hospital into a secure cloud, extracts markers of seizure risk, sleep, and medication level in real time, and connects all of it to an AI the patient can text with from their phone. The AI checks in with short surveys, sends alerts when it detects seizures or interictal spikes, answers questions like how did I sleep last night? with real data and plots, and records what patients report back. Those reports become labels that retrain the seizure detector, so the system gets better at recognizing each person's seizures the longer they communicate.

Our pilot study enrolled 13 patients in Penn's epilepsy monitoring unit. The study is soon to be published in Nature Medicine. Since then, close to 50 patients have used the system, with enrollment ongoing. We are working to bring it out of the hospital and into daily life with sub-scalp EEG and DBS devices.
details: The platform has three main components. On the hospital side, real-time clinical EEG is relayed, along with medication logs, into Azure Event Hubs. In the cloud, Databricks streaming pipelines preprocess the signal and run pretrained models for seizure detection (SPaRCNet for scalp EEG, WaveNet and ONCET for intracranial), interictal spike detection, and sleep staging (YASA), plus brain-wide phase synchrony and an estimate of anti-seizure medication load derived from dosing records. Results land in Delta tables in a Unity Catalog. The patient-facing app is a Flask service on Azure App Service backed by PostgreSQL, installed as a progressive web app.

The conversational AI is a LangGraph state machine. Every incoming message passes through a moderation node, then a router decides whether it is general conversation or a question about the patient's data. Data questions go to a ReAct-style agent that inspects the database schema, writes SQL against that patient's records, and synthesizes an answer. Every AI response is moderated again before delivery, and investigators reviewed all conversations daily. The model was a HIPAA-compliant deployment of GPT-4o-mini.

2025-2026.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces Competition Website
2025-2026.blurb: A class competition site for decoding finger movements from brain recordings.
body: Brain-Computer Interfaces (BE 5210) is Penn's graduate BCI course, and its final project is a competition. Student teams receive electrocorticography recordings from patients who were flexing their fingers while wearing a data glove, and the teams have to build models that predict the finger movements from the brain signals alone. Teams register, upload their prediction files, and are scored automatically against held-out data. Scores are only revealed on a fixed schedule, creating a competitive dynamic where teams vie for leaderboard rankings against increasingly difficult accuracy thresholds. This website was previously held together by many years of hotfixes and code duct tape, with a single CSV file as the foundation of the site. This year, I completely redesigned and rebuilt the website, with modern cloud infrastructure and services. Of course, I added some easter eggs for the students to find :)
details: The stack is a React frontend, a Flask API, and PostgreSQL, containerized with Docker. Submissions are parsed with SciPy from .mat files, validated for the expected variable and shape, and scored as the correlation between predicted and actual finger flexion. The frontend deploys to S3 behind CloudFront and the API runs on Elastic Beanstalk with RDS for the database, all defined in Terraform.

The leaderboard refresh is a database-backed timer. A scheduled job checks whether the next release time has passed and, in a single transaction, publishes pending scores and advances the timer, so the leaderboard moves exactly once per interval even with several API workers running. The interval is configurable through environment variables, which let it tighten from every three hours to hourly as deadlines approach.

2025-2026.title: Sociail Chat
2025-2026.blurb: Bringing together the best of human and AI collaboration.
body: My time at Sociail marks my first true entrepreneurial experience. I joined the founding team right after graduating from Drexel and developed the initial prototype of Sociail Chat, our collaborative AI platform. As the startup grew, I found myself leading a multinational software development team and guiding the product through successive iterations until a limited release. Approaching launch, my focus shifted from technical development to product design, user experience, and go-to-market strategy. My co-founder responsibilities helped build the company itself: interviewing and onboarding team members, establishing our culture, and creating the 'operating system' of Sociail. There is so much more to share, and eventually I'll write something long-form that conveys how truly foundational this experience is.

2024-2025.title: AskEEG
2024-2025.blurb: Ask questions about brain recordings and get analyses back.
body: Final project for Biomedical Informatics (BMIN 5100) at Penn. Analyzing EEG usually means manually writing code to select a time window, set of channels, calculate a feature of interest (e.g. a specific frequency band), and plot it — all before you can begin to understand your data. AskEEG replaces that tedious process with a natural language interface that enables EEG data exploration and analysis just by asking for it. A researcher can type "What is the synchrony in the alpha band from 10 to 20 seconds?" and the app uses a large language model to extract the parameters, run the analysis on the recording, and return the results and plots. This is a complete cloud application running on AWS and was my first experience developing with infrastructure as code.
details: The large language model (GPT-4o mini through LangChain) reads the question, picks the feature of interest from the app's toolbox of analyses, and extracts its parameters: time window, frequency band, and channels. The app then computes that feature in Python. For synchrony, for instance, the recording is re-referenced to the common average, notch-filtered to remove 60 Hz line noise, and bandpass-filtered to the requested band. The Hilbert transform gives each channel's instantaneous phase, and the Kuramoto order parameter turns those phases into a single number between 0 and 1 that captures how synchronized the channels are at each moment. Results come back as time series plots and per-band summaries.

The frontend is Vue 3 with Pinia, backend is a Flask REST API. Recording metadata comes from Pennsieve and the data itself from S3. The compute-heavy analysis runs in Docker containers on AWS Fargate, with logs in CloudWatch and the infrastructure defined in Terraform.

2024-2025.title: ASM Calc
2024-2025.org: Penn Center for Neuroengineering and Therapeutics
2024-2025.blurb: Calculate and visualize anti-seizure medication (ASM) levels over time using pharmacokinetic modeling.
body: In the epilepsy monitoring unit, clinicians deliberately lower a patient's ASM levels to provoke seizures they can record and localize. The taper strategy is critical to this process, but is often done by feel rather than with quantitative methods. ASM Calc is a small tool I built with clinicians at Penn to help plan those tapers and avoid severe seizures. Clinicians enter each dose and the time it was given, and it models the estimated concentration of every drug over time, plus the combined total when several are active. The estimates come from a pharmacokinetic model developed in our lab and published in Epilepsia.
details: Nineteen common ASMs are pre-configured with literature-sourced half-life, volume of distribution, and bioavailability, all of which can be adjusted. Each dose is modeled with first-order absorption and elimination, so its curve rises as the drug is absorbed and decays with the drug's half-life, and overlapping doses are summed.
The frontend is React with Vite and the API is Flask, deployed as Vercel serverless functions.

2024-2025.title: EpiTracker
body: Final project for Applied Medical Innovation, where we learned and executed the process of creating impactful, commercially viable medical innovations. The concept for EpiTracker emerged from nearly a dozen stakeholder interviews spanning neurologists, neurosurgeons, foundations, and patients, with the goal of identifying addressable gaps in epilepsy care. We discovered an opportunity to reduce the time to optimal treatment by capturing critical information from ambulatory settings and presenting actionable trends and insights to support clinical care decisions. The project culminated in a functional prototype of EpiTracker—which took the form of a mobile app for patients and web portal for clinicians—and a final pitch complete with market research and a business model.

2024-2025.title: Custom Hardline Liquid Cooled PC
2024-2025.blurb: My first foray into building liquid cooled computers.
body: I've been building computers for over a decade (since I was 14 years old). In fact, it was this skill that landed me my first job as an assistant technician at a local IT company. As a kid, I loved to disassemble old tech products to see what was inside — although I had no idea how any of it worked. But going the other direction to build something functional was a whole new paradigm. I did figure it out though, because that first computer I built is still next to me, and still running! Since then, I've built computers for friends, several machine learning servers, and now my second (and first ever liquid cooled) PC. This build was significantly more challenging, but worth it for the experience gain and seeing the meticulous planning finally come together. There are a couple things to improve: my 90° bends could use some practice and one of the GPU tubing runs will need to be re-routed next time I do maintenance. Overall, I'm proud of this build and glad I took it on.

2023-2024.title: Evaluation of Cognitive Function using Time-Domain Optical Neuroimaging
2023-2024.blurb: Master's thesis research project under Dr. Hasan Ayaz.
body: For my master's thesis, I investigated a miniaturized time-domain functional near-infrared spectroscopy (TD-fNIRS) neuroimaging system, Kernel Flow, for assessing the neural correlates of cognitive function. This was the first comprehensive cognitive study using TD-fNIRS and whole-head optical brain monitoring, as well as the first cognitive study with Kernel Flow. Through this project, I developed and verified an experimental setup for investigating the neural correlates of cognitive tasks and designed open-source tools to facilitate optical neuroimaging research.

2023-2024.title: Novel Medical Devices for Neurocritical Care Monitoring
2023-2024.blurb: Capturing contextual data and environmental factors in the neuro-ICU.
body: In collaboration with UT Southwestern Medical Center, I designed and developed devices to capture intracranial pressure (ICP) context as well as light, temperature, and noise levels in neuro-ICU rooms. After the Stopcock Position Sensor for ICP context was clinically validated at UT Southwestern Medical Center, I initiated a joint effort with a Drexel Senior Design team to overhaul the devices and verify the sensors for environmental data capture.

2022-2023.title: Neurocritical Care Patient Outcome Predictor
2022-2023.blurb: A GUI-based tool for clinicians to predict the outcome of a neurocritical care patient.
body: Final project for the Advanced Biocomputational Languages graduate class taught by Dr. Ahmet Sacan. We created a GUI for clinicians that predicts the outcome of a neurocritical care patient. The parameters input for the current patient are compared to a database of retrospectively collected patient and medical data using a k-nearest neighbors algorithm. The utilized database is the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-IV.

2022-2023.title: TrachTalk
2022-2023.blurb: An independently operable pediatric tracheostomy cuff controller.
body: Junior Design project for a device that inflates or deflates a tracheostomy cuff at the press of a button. The inflation pressure is set by a clinician using the dial and is maintained while the patient is breathing. The patient presses the button when he or she wishes to speak and the cuff deflates. This work was presented at several Drexel Biomed events at which I participated on a Q&A panel for prospective students.

2022-2023.title: BrainTech Podcast
2022-2023.blurb: I hosted and produced the BrainTech Podcast.
body: Through conversations with researchers, engineers, business leaders, and thinkers in brain technology, I hope to inspire students who will shape the future of this field. This podcast was spun out of the Brain Technology Convergence graduate course taught by Dr. Banu Onaral. Four episodes were created as an initial run. I would like to return to this project at some point and do more with the BrainTech channel.

2021-2022.title: Real-Time EEG-Based BCI Motor Imagery Classifier
2021-2022.blurb: Acquires 8-channel EEG data from the OpenBCI Ultracortex Mark IV headset, creates left vs. right-hand motor imagery datasets, and classifies user intention in near real-time.
body: Final project for the Neural Networks graduate course taught by Dr. Hualou Liang. We evaluated the classification accuracies of several convolutional neural network models from the Army Research Laboratory (ARL) EEGModels project and then trained our own to classify motor imagery intention from my OpenBCI headset. The software handles EEG data acquisition from the headset, pre-processing, and visualization, as well as dataset creation and real-time classification using our model.

2020-2021.title: NeoPET
2020-2021.blurb: The Novel application for Parkinson's and Essential Tremor (NeoPET) provides an innovative way of tracking Parkinson's and Essential Tremor symptoms and treatment responses through a smartphone.
body: Collaborated with students from UMN to create a mobile app for Parkinson's and Essential Tremor patients that uses machine learning to analyze and quantify symptom severity. We leveraged accelerometer, gyroscope, and keystroke data streams from a smartphone to train the model and create visualizations for clinicians to remotely monitor disease progression over time. Built on Android and Google Firebase.
